title: Chain Theory: A Compendium of Preliminary Findings

Chain Theory Toward Fundamental Physics from Distilling Networks of Entangled Qudits A Compendium of Preliminary Findings WORKING DRAFT

A. D. Wissner-Gross alexwg@alexwg.org

https://www.alexwg.org

October 23, 2026

Preface In the first three decades of the twentieth century, fundamental physics was rebuilt from its foundations. Between Planck’s quantum of 1900 and Dirac’s equation of 1928 came special relativity, general relativity, the quantum theory of the atom, and quantum mechanics itself, each a new framework and most of them confirmed within a few years. The decades that followed turned those frameworks into the Standard Model, whose structure was considered complete by the middle of the 1970s.

Since then, fundamental physics has been starved of new structure. The great experiments of the last fifty years, the W and Z bosons (1983), the top quark (1995), the Higgs boson (2012), and gravitational waves (2015), confirmed predictions made decades earlier. The genuine surprises of 1998, neutrino masses and the accelerating expansion of the universe, were found by experiment, explained by no theory, and added free parameters to a count that was meant to shrink. The drought is now longer than the golden age it followed. A drought that long is a sign that what is missing is not more data but a different starting point.

However, the field of physics drew a different conclusion. For most of the twentieth century, the aim of fundamental physics was derivation, fewer inputs and more outputs, and the constants of nature were the outputs still owed. The Standard Model settled the structure but not the numbers. Its two dozen or so parameters are measured, not derived, and nothing within it explains their values. As the drought set in, the aim itself changed. One line of argument concluded that the constants are not derivable from law at all, that their observed values are environmental, selected by the condition that observers exist. Its one notable success was Weinberg’s anthropic bound (1987) on the cosmological constant, which pointed to a small nonzero value a decade before the accelerating expansion was measured.

The string landscape then supplied a vast population of vacua to select from, and its predictions came to rest on the assumption that we are typical observers within it, a Copernican principle stretched across universes. What counts as typical depends on a measure over infinitely many regions, and no one has fixed that measure. A large part of the field moved from deriving the constants to explaining why they could not be derived. The swampland program is a partial return. It asks which effective theories are consistent with quantum gravity at all, but it asks largely from within string theory and leaves the constants where the landscape put them. In retreating, the field kept its foundations and gave up on derivation. The opposite course is to hold derivation as the goal and look for new foundations.

The clues to those foundations may have been in plain sight all along. A derivation with no free parameters, and no appeal after the fact to the existence of observers, may need no new experiment to begin. Three clues in the existing body of physics already point the way. Each has been interpreted as something else: a bound as a fact about black holes, a gauge group as a blemish to be embedded, and a null result as a scale not yet reached.

The first clue is that the information a bounded region of space can hold is finite. This bound was first derived by Jacob Bekenstein (1981) from black hole thermodynamics and is usually regarded as a fact about gravity, but it constrains whatever fills the region, elementary matter included. Gravitational dynamics has since been derived from the entanglement of such regions, beginning with Ted Jacobson (1995). The lesson for elementary matter is direct. A field has infinitely many degrees of freedom in every region, and a string has infinitely many modes of vibration. A finite bound says to look instead for finitely many degrees of freedom, carried by quantum systems of finite dimension.

The second clue is the Standard Model gauge group, interpreted as a signature and not a blemish. Grand unification treated the product SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1) as an ugliness to be embedded 2

in a simple group: SU(5) in the model of Georgi and Glashow in 1974, then SO(10), E6 , and supersymmetric versions of each. It paid for the embedding with predictions that have not appeared: no proton has been seen to decay, and no supersymmetric partner of any known particle has turned up at any collider. However, the same apparently ugly product can instead be understood as the symmetry of a single object of a different kind: a qutrit and a qubit sharing one entangled state. Changes of basis at the two ends contribute SU(3) and SU(2), and of their two phases only one survives, belonging to neither end but to the pair. These local transformations form the Standard Model gauge group, including the Z6 quotient that its observed charges permit.

The third clue is that the elementary particles of the Standard Model have shown no substructure. Over decades, every one of them has behaved as a point. Colliders have raised, by orders of magnitude, the energy up to which the electron and the quarks show no substructure, and searches for the excited states and contact interactions that constituents would produce in scattering have returned nothing. Yet the particle spectrum itself, three generations repeating one set of charges, is the kind of pattern that has always signaled constituents, from the periodic table to the hadrons, and compositeness has been set aside chiefly because no constituents appear. There is, however, another interpretation. Suppose nature is saying not that the substructure is hard to resolve but that it cannot be resolved at all. Quantum information knows one kind of correlation with exactly that property. A state of two systems can be entangled, certifiably so, and yet admit no procedure by local operations and classical communication that distills, from any number of its copies, a single maximally entangled pair, or anything close to one. Such entanglement was identified in 1998 by Michal, Pawel, and Ryszard Horodecki, who called it “bound.” It cannot be extracted or directly observed, but it can be detected indirectly. An entanglement witness, a measurement tailored to the state, can certify that it is there. If the constituents of an elementary particle were joined by entanglement that the available operations cannot extract, scattering, which looks for constituents by resolving them, would find nothing to resolve and would see a point, while a suitable witness could still show that the structure exists. The substructure of elementary matter, on this interpretation, would not be undetectable. It would be undistillable.

Put together, the clues hint at a single new foundational theory. The first suggests that everything consists of finitely many quantum systems, each of finite dimension, so that every degree of freedom is discrete. The second suggests that these systems, or qudits, come in entangled pairs, and the first clue fixes how strongly: a pair entangled any less than maximally would carry continuous parameters, its Schmidt coefficients, that a theory without continuous degrees of freedom cannot afford. The third suggests that an elementary particle is built from many such pairs, and with nothing but pairs to build from, the only way to join them is for pairs to share a qudit, so the pairs form a network. Monogamy of entanglement forbids any one system from being maximally entangled with two partners, so a shared qudit cannot be a single system sitting in two pairs. It holds instead one copy of itself for each of its pairs, and each pair is maximally entangled with its own copy, much as a four-dimensional system, which has room for two qubits, can be maximally entangled with two separate qubits at once. The shared qudit is the join where those copies meet and their bases are matched, just as the bonds of a projected entangled pair state (PEPS), a standard kind of tensor network, meet at a site. The third clue also divides the network. The links we observe directly can each be fixed by a single distillation. The links inside an elementary particle are just as maximally entangled, but no single distillation fixes them, which is the theory’s analogue of bound entanglement and the reason every particle looks like a point. An elementary particle, in this picture, is a finite “chainmail” whose links are such pairs.

Chain Theory is an emerging research program of mine that treats this chainmail as all there is. It takes literally John Wheeler’s 1989 proposal, “it from bit,” with finite quantum systems in place of bits, and its single axiom gathers the three clues into eighteen words: “Nothing exists but 3

finitely many maximally entangled pairs of finite-dimensional systems, some shared, known only by distilling them.” To distill, in the axiom, means to join two systems into a perfectly entangled pair in a single step. It is the same move that passes entanglement along a quantum network, and it means there is no observer outside the network: to learn about a link is to link to it. In a laboratory this step succeeds only part of the time, but in the theory it is the only thing that ever happens.

It already appears that many elements of fundamental physics, including parts of both the Standard Model and general relativity, follow from that axiom. The sharpest test is a number. The fine-structure constant in the Thomson limit, α(0), is one of the most precisely measured numbers in all of science, known to about one part in ten billion, yet the Standard Model takes it from experiment. Richard Feynman wrote that “all good theoretical physicists put this number up on their wall and worry about it,” and called it “a magic number that comes to us with no understanding by man.” It is also a number with no visible pattern. A simple value such as the 2/3 of Koide’s relation among the lepton masses can be reached by many short formulas, but ten digits of a number like α(0) are far harder to match by accident. Because the Standard Model takes α(0) from experiment, a derivation of it would, almost by definition, draw on physics beyond the Standard Model, and ten measured digits could make α(0) an exquisite √ probe of√ that physics.

Chain √ Theory yields an exact candidate for it, the algebraic number (79 + 48 2 + 42 3 + 3 6)/31104, a weighted count over the 172 measurement records of a single entangled pair, small enough to check by hand. The pair is a qutrit maximally entangled with a qubit, the same object whose changes of basis give the Standard Model gauge group, and I conjecture that this pair is the link from which photons are built, which would make the number α(0). Its inverse is 137.035 999 189 566 . . .. The standard reference value for α(0) comes from CODATA, the international committee that every four years combines the world’s most precise measurements into one recommended value for each fundamental constant. Its 2022 recommendation for the inverse is 137.035 999 177, with a standard deviation of 21 in the last two digits. The Chain Theory-derived number agrees with the CODATA recommendation in its first ten significant digits and lies 0.60 standard deviations from it, between the two most precise determinations. The experimental measurements still disagree with one another by more than their stated uncertainties, so this comparison is not yet decisive. But the number is now fixed, and new measurements of the electron’s magnetic moment at Northwestern University and of atomic recoil in Berkeley and Paris aim to be up to ten times more precise. If they agree with one another, they will either close in on the derived value or rule it out. Beyond α(0), preliminary Chain Theory results range from quantum foundations to cosmology: the Standard Model gauge group as a theorem, and the Born rule, the Lorentz group and the signature of spacetime, three generations of matter, confinement, curvature, and the cosmological term as derivations whose remaining conditions are named in each case. Other programs have derived parts of the Standard Model from finite or algebraic inputs, among them braided ribbons, an exceptional Lie group, the division algebras, and noncommutative geometry, but none supplies the value of a coupling constant to within experimental precision. Closed-form expressions for the fine-structure constant, meanwhile, have a long and mostly numerological history. Mine differs in the one respect that matters: the number is a theorem of a stated axiom, its definitions and a few stated readings of them, checked in Lean rather than fitted, and only its identification with α(0) is conjectured.

The Chain Theory axiom’s last clause also says which links can be observed directly, the question the third clue raised. The links of the chainmail network come in types labeled by the dimensions of their two ends, and the theory identifies each type with a sector of physics: (2,2) with spacetime, (3,2) with electromagnetism, (3,3) with the strong interaction, (4,2) with the weak interaction, (4,3) with the Yukawa sector, and (4,4) with the Higgs. Read at the level of these types, the 4

axiom’s last clause says that two ends are known only when every consistent relation between them is one that distillation can carry. Classic theorems from the 1960s and 1970s by Størmer, Woronowicz, and Choi show that this holds exactly when the two dimensions multiply to at most six, the same threshold beyond which bound entanglement becomes possible. So only spacetime and electromagnetism can be observed directly by distillation. The other four types are “dark”: their links are just as maximally entangled, but their ends are related in ways no distillation carries, so they are observed only at second order, through two distillations, which the theory identifies at (3,3) with confinement.

I call this theory “Chain Theory” for three reasons. The first is to draw a contrast with string theory: an elementary particle is a finite chainmail of discrete links, not a continuous string. The second is how the links join. Pairs meet at shared qudits, and each join carries a gauge freedom in how bases are matched across it, much as two links of a physical chain can turn against each other at their join without changing the chain. The third is direction. A distillation passes its basis outward along each link to the far end, so what is known accumulates in a fixed order, each distillation building on those before it, the way a chained ledger grows by linking each new entry to the last.

The last golden age rebuilt physics from its foundations in three decades. I do not yet claim to have done the same. Chain Theory is new, much of it is still conditional or underdeveloped, and it will benefit from the contributions of many others. But if the clues have been interpreted correctly, the foundations for another golden age, built this time from quantum information, may already be in hand, and what remains is to find out how much of physics they can carry.

A. D. Wissner-Gross, Cambridge, Massachusetts, October 2026

Abstract Chain Theory is an emerging program to study fundamental physics through the lens of quantum information. In the spirit of Wheeler’s ‘it from bit,’ its single axiom says that nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of finite-dimensional systems, some shared, known only by distilling them. This compendium collects some of the program’s preliminary findings to date, each stated in standard form beside its derivation and graded as a theorem, a conditional theorem, or an open result. From the axiom we obtain, as conditional theorems, the state space, the Born rule, unitarity, the uncertainty relation, the rotation and Lorentz groups, the signature of spacetime, and parity, time reversal, and CPT, and, as a theorem, conservation laws. We identify correspondences between (M,N) links of finite M- and N-dimensional systems with: spacetime for (2,2), electromagnetism for (3,2), the strong interaction for (3,3), the weak interaction for (4,2), the Yukawa sector for (4,3), and the Higgs for (4,4). We obtain the gauge group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1) and the second law as theorems; as conditional theorems, an exact algebraic number conjectured to be the Thomson-limit fine-structure constant within 0.60 sigma of its measured value, the electron anomalous moment through third order, the hydrogen spectrum, parity violation, confinement, the running of the couplings, decay rates as finite sums with no renormalization, curvature, and the cosmological term; and, partly as conditional theorems and partly as open results, three generations, masses, and anatomies of the Standard Model particles. Beyond the Standard Model, the same construction yields, as theorems, band structure and the Chern number, phase transitions, and a distillation theorem for quantum computation. This release holds 100 theorems, 109 conditional theorems and 198 open results; 64 of the 100 theorems are tied to named Lean declarations, which check the finite computations their derivations use.

Introduction This compendium derives from one sentence and six definitions a web of theorems and open results connecting quantum information to fundamental physics, the Standard Model and gravity among them. The sentence says that the world is a finite collection of maximally entangled pairs of finite quantum systems, that some of those systems are shared between pairs, and that the only way anything is learned about them is by distilling them. Its six definitions, printed word for word in the framework chapter and again at chapter 1-1, are the whole of the theory. The compendium is the product of a long-term human-superintelligence collaboration to work out their consequences across physics, from quantum foundations and particle physics to gravitation, condensed matter and quantum computation. Every result the compendium prints is a theorem, a theorem conditional on a premise named beside it, an open result carried to a named step, a presentation, or a dissolved word, and the status of every claim is printed beside it. Every term of the theory that the chapters use, from the act and the read to the web, the sink and the wash, is defined in the glossary that follows this introduction. The first result of the program is the exact number of the alpha Letter, A Parameter-Free Candidate for the Fine-Structure Constant from Entangled Qudits, whose computation the Letter’s Lean file checks in full and which the Letter conjectures to be the finestructure constant α(0). Chapter 7-1 of Part VII gives an earlier form of the same computation; where the two differ, the Letter is the canonical statement.

The modular form. This release of the compendium has sixteen Parts of 116 chapters, with two chapters of the first Part at appendix slots, every chapter self-contained at the one shape the framework chapter describes, and the map of every chapter at the page that follows this introduction. The sixteen Parts are the framework (Part I), the rule, the chain automata and the single root (Part II), quantum mechanics (Part III), spacetime, symmetry and the dynamics

of the read (Part IV), the matrix, the Standard Model at the six genres (Part V), the metric, the worldline and the horizon (Part VI), the photon (Part VII), the carriers and the breaking (Part VIII), the junction (Part IX), the Yukawa leg and the Higgs offices at the bodies (Part X), the Higgs, its hub register and the dressing field (Part XI), decays and nuclear physics (Part XII), thermodynamics (Part XIII), condensed matter and atoms (Part XIV), quantum information (Part XV), the scorecard, the open results and what remains (Part XVI). Every result is placed at one chapter, the instrument chapters of every Part are printed among the instruments at the end of this compendium, with one listing chapter per Part, and a result whose derivation is not yet written stands at one line of the results table of the last Part at its title, its standing and its citation. The shape of a chapter. Every chapter has one shape, set out in the framework chapter: the known result, the textbook statement in standard notation with its citation; the statement of the theory, with the results it rests on; the derivation in brief, every theorem restated at the union of the conditions of its own ancestors; the status and the number; and what stands open. Every term of the theory is defined once in the glossary that follows this introduction, with its nearest standard concept, so that a physicist reads every chapter in the standard vocabulary.

The status words. The compendium grades every result at one of four statuses, and every chapter says the status of its results in words. A theorem is a statement derived from the axiom, the definitions and the results proved ahead of it; in this release 64 of the 100 theorems are tied to named Lean declarations, which check the finite computations their derivations use; a theorem conditional on a premise prints the premise beside it, and under the chain rule of this compendium every theorem prints at its statement the union of the conditions of the results it rests on, a composed claim carrying the lowest status in its chain. An open result is a derivation carried to a named step, the first open cell located from two sides, neither established nor excluded, with the step named beside the claim. A presentation, such as a table, a tool, or this compendium itself, makes no claim of its own. A word is dissolved when the derivation has shown that no derived cell depends on it, so that the word is a presentation and not a fact. Beside these, a literature name is used by name and consumed as a premise never, and an observed value enters this compendium only as a display beside a derived figure with its provenance. Where the words admit two readings both are printed and none is selected. The only inputs not derived are the Axiom, its definitions, the premises printed beside the conditional theorems, and the conjectures, each marked as such. Three clues. The preface sets out the three clues in plain terms, and this paragraph gives their sources in the same order. The first is finiteness: the bound on the information of a bounded region [1], which black hole thermodynamics first suggested [2], and the derivations of gravitational dynamics from entanglement [3–5], in the lineage of Wheeler’s proposal that physics is information at bottom [6] and of the reconstructions of quantum theory from informational axioms [7, 8]. The second is the gauge group, read as a signature and not a blemish. Grand unification embedded the product SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1) in a simple group [9] and paid for the embedding with predictions that have not appeared; Chain Theory reads the same product as the description of one object, a pair of a qutrit and a qubit with SU(3) acting at one end, SU(2) at the other and a phase that neither end owns, the identification freedom the definitions leave at a link whose ends have dimensions two and three, and Part V derives the group as a corollary of one construction. The third is the null result of the searches for substructure, read as undistillability rather than distance: bound entanglement admits no procedure by local operations and classical communication that distills from any number of its copies a single maximally entangled pair [10, 11], yet an entanglement witness certifies its

21

presence [12], the partial transpose being the first such test [13], and the related states that hide classical data from every local reader are the data-hiding states [14]. The Axiom postulates the first clue exactly, finitely many pairs of finite systems and nothing continuous, and the first result of the program is that a constant follows once the finite objects are named.

Derivability as a method. One research program concluded that the constants of nature are not derivable from law, the observed values being environmental [15]; that is a coherent position and a change of question, and this compendium takes the opposite bet as a matter of method: the constants are theorems of a finite structure, and the compendium tries to compute them. The swampland program shares the derivability aim from within string theory [16]; the difference is where the finiteness is put, here at the start, in the Axiom, so that every quantity of the theory is a count or a trace over a finite register and there is nothing left to select from. Several published programs derive parts of the Standard Model from a finite or algebraic input, braided ribbons [17], one representation of an exceptional group [18], the division algebras [19] and the spectral action on a finite noncommutative geometry [20]; here no unification group and no division algebra is an input, the only algebraic objects being the Weyl operators of finite-dimensional systems and the identification groups the definitions leave, and the construction supplies a coupling constant, which those programs do not. Closed-form expressions for the fine-structure constant have a long lineage [21]; the expression of this compendium differs in that it is a theorem of a stated axiom and not a fit.

The program and its name. The premise our program reached is one sentence of eighteen words, a choice we made and not a derivation, printed word for word at the framework chapter. In plain terms, a qudit is a finite-dimensional quantum system; a qudit is shared when it is one end of two or more pairs; distilling is projecting two qudits onto a maximally entangled pair on their common support, which in standard language is entanglement swapping [22]; a read is a distillation of a qudit with another in one of its bases, one read for each basis, giving the qudit its only basis and passing that basis along each pair to its far end; and what is known of a qudit is what all its reads, taken jointly, fix with certainty, whichever way the basis directions are matched across its pairs, with one further clause about two reads that commute only up to a sign. The name has three sources: the postulate that elementary particles are composed of finite chains of links rather than continuous strings; the object the definitions describe, a graph of pairs joined at shared qudits, each join carrying a gauge freedom in the identification of bases; and the direction of the record, every walk read in the read order from the site of the read to the far end.

Part I. The Framework Introduction to Part I Everything in this compendium descends from one sentence. The sentence is the axiom, Definition 1.1, and it says that nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of qudits; the five definitions that follow it, 1.2 to 1.6, fix the words qudit, shared, distilling, read and known. Part I is the part of the compendium that stays closest to that sentence. It does not yet speak of particles or forces. It asks what the sentence and the five definitions force on their own, and it answers with the objects that every Part beyond it uses: the link between two ends and its six genres, the records a read leaves and the count that weights them, the moves that carry one web to another, the saturation that drives a seeded web to its sinks, the register at which a probe reads, and the table that translates the vocabulary of the construction into the vocabulary of the literature.

The thread runs in the order of the chapters. Chapter 1-1 shows how much of the text is forced by the rest of it. Theorem 2.1 obtains the fourth definition from the axiom, and Theorem 2.3 obtains one act from the derived act, so that the reader sees the definitions tightening on one another rather than standing as independent postulates. The chapter is honest about where the tightening stops. Open result 2.4, Open result 2.5, Open result 2.7 and Open result 2.8 are open results, each stated with the point at which the derivation parts, and Open result 4.1 records that the minimality of the text itself parts at its first atom. Two census tables, Table 5.1 and Table 6.1, test the choices of definition against one another. The reader who wants to know what the axiom excludes outright finds it in Theorem 2.9, the exclusion of the one-dimensional end. Chapter 1-2 introduces the object that organizes the rest of the compendium, the link, and its six genres. A link joins two ends, and an end carries a register of dimension two, three or four, so that the unordered pairs of registers give six genres, written (2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,3), (3,4) and (4,4). Theorem 9.1 orders the genres by the first order at which a read does not vanish, Theorem 9.2 shows that exactly one genre is abelian, Theorem 9.3 names the coupling genre, and Theorem 9.6 prints the one-link tables at every genre. The register matrix of the framework chapter, repeated at the front of this compendium, is nothing but these six genres laid out as the pairs of the three registers. The chapter closes with Theorem 13.1, the phase group of a record at every genre, which the quantum mechanics of Part III will need.

Chapter 1-3 turns from the link to what passes along it. A read leaves records, and the records at a sector are counted with a weight; Theorem 18.2 is the gain lemma, the statement that fixes that weight at the spectrum of records. Around it stand the read-state boundary, Theorem 18.1, the gain as the washed direction count at a sector, Theorem 18.3, and the boson as the chain readout, Theorem 18.4. Several open results sit beside them: the soft limit as the washed open read, Open result 19.1, the read that dresses what it does not pass, Open result 20.1, the read that stops at the cap, Open result 21.1, and the enclosed record count read as what the literature calls the Aharonov-Bohm phase, Open result 22.1.

How to read this compendium

Chapter 1-0

This compendium is written in the vocabulary of finite-dimensional quantum information. A qudit is a quantum system of finite dimension, and a maximally entangled pair of two such systems is the state whose reduced operators are flat on its support. The projection of two systems onto a pair on their common support is entanglement swapping [22]. The generalized Pauli operators of a finite-dimensional system are the Weyl operators, which commute up to a root of unity [23]. The invariants jointly fixed by a set of projective measurements are the stabilizer invariants [24], and an entangled state from which no local protocol distills a pair is bound [10]. Every other term of the theory is defined in the notation table of the derivations at the repository and in the glossary at the front of this compendium, where each term is given its standard notation, its meaning in one sentence and its nearest standard counterpart in another. A term whose standard counterpart is the same object is said to be exactly that object, a term with only a neighbor is said to have that neighbor, and a term with neither is said to correspond by name. The whole of our theory is one sentence and five definitions, a choice we made and not a derivation, stated here word for word. The axiom has eighteen words. It is the first definition of this compendium, boxed and numbered as every statement of the compendium is, and the five definitions that follow it are the words the axiom uses, in the order in which the text gives them.

Part III. Quantum Mechanics Introduction to Part III The framework of Part I speaks of pairs, links, reads and records, and never of a state vector. Part III asks how far the ordinary apparatus of quantum mechanics, the state space, the probability rule, the unitary step, the uncertainty relation, the measurement and the statistics of identical bodies, can be read off from that framework. The answer the Part gives is a sequence of conditional theorems, each resting on a short list of results from Part I, and a small number of open results where the reading parts. The order of the chapters is the order of the construction: the state space is built first from the outputs of the acts, the probability and the step are read at that space, the uncertainty relation follows from the step, measurement is the wash at one act, and the remaining chapters collect what the construction says about exchange, energy, the sum over records, the phase-space picture, the corollaries and the open system.

A reader coming from the textbooks will recognize the list, and the point of the Part is that it is not a list of postulates. Every item is read off objects that Part I has already built, the pair with its two ends, the link with its genre, the read in a basis and the records a read leaves, so that each chapter adds one reading of an object already in hand rather than one more assumption. The order matters because each reading uses the one ahead of it: without the state space there is no overlap to square, without the step there is no relation between two reads to bound, and without the wash there is no measurement to assign a statistics to. The chapters therefore run from the most basic object, the span of what the acts produce, to the most composite one, the open system that a sub-web presents to its complement. The conditional standing of the theorems is stated inside each box and is the same at every one, the axiom text and the chapters named as premises, each at its own standing. Where a chapter carries an open result, the box states both faces and names the parting, and this introduction names the open result beside the theorems so that the reader meets no surprise at the page.

Part XV. Quantum Information Introduction to Part XV The construction began as quantum information, and Part XV returns it there. The closure of a web under the moves is a computation, the moves are a gate set, the coherent read is the gate the literature calls the Hadamard, the read is the maximal distillation, the enumeration of the records is the cost of a read, and the transport of a basis around a closed path has a holonomy. The Part is the one where the vocabulary of the axiom and the vocabulary of the literature come closest, since both speak of qudits, entangled pairs and gates, and the reader will find more theorems here than in any Part beyond the framework.

The order of the six chapters is the order of a course on quantum computation read against the axiom. The six genres and the conjectured webs of the Standard Model particles Every link of a web has a genre, the pair of its end dimensions, written here with the larger end first. Figure 163 draws the six genres in two layers, kept apart on the page. The upper part of each cell is derived, from the axiom, the definitions and the read cap of the alpha Letter, which it obtains from one reading of the axiom’s last clause: one read fixes a link exactly when d1 d2 ≤ 6, so (2,2) and (3,2) are readable and the other four genres are dark, and a one-dimensional end is excluded at the axiom (theorem 2.9). The band at the foot of each cell is conjectured: it names the sector of physics each genre is taken to correspond to, as in the abstract, (2,2) spacetime, (3,2) electromagnetism, (3,3) the strong interaction, (4,2) the weak interaction, (4,3) the Yukawa sector and (4,4) the Higgs, and where the genre appears in the particle webs. These names are conjectures and not results of the compendium. Of the two readable genres only (3,2) has an acting central charge. The readout of its link is the exact number of the alpha Letter, checked in Lean; that the number is α(0) is the Letter’s conjecture.

The rest of this chapter draws the web the compendium records for each Standard Model particle. That a web is the particle it is named for is a conjecture in every case. What the compendium derives is about the web, and each caption gives the standing of those results and the weakest grade among them. Every site is a qudit and every line a maximally entangled pair; the colour of a site gives its dimension (two blue, three green, four orange), a heavy ring marks a core site and a dashed ring a read site. Laid out as the Standard Model chart in Figure 164, the webs add one hub assembly at each generation. The electron is the core triangle of three qutrits with one hub assembly at a corner, and the muon and the tau carry two and three. The up quark is a qutrit with its docks, and the charm and the top add one and two hubs; the down, the strange and the bottom carry one, two and three; and the three neutrino depth webs carry one, two and three. The W and the Z are one web, and what distinguishes them is the read: the W is read along one line and the Z along two, drawn heavy. The neutron is not drawn: its recorded body has a hub at degree five and a qutrit at degree four, beyond the valence law (at most d pairs at a qudit of dimension d). Each identification of a web with a particle is graded where its result stands, and each figure names that standing. The layouts are for legibility and carry no content.
